annotations.keyFindings: Median time from call to first critical intervention fell from 11.2 to 8.4 minutes after monthly in-situ simulation in one hospital; unplanned intensive care admission did not change.
annotations.limitations: No control; a new early warning score and team turnover in the same period.

annotations.keyFindings: Across five hospitals and 6,480 calls, time to first critical intervention fell by a median 3.1 minutes; unplanned intensive care admission did not change (odds ratio 0.96); simulations were cancelled in 14 percent of planned months.
annotations.limitations: Five clusters gave imprecise between-hospital estimates; staggered order but open delivery.

synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. In-situ simulation for rapid response teams was followed by shorter times to the first critical intervention in one uncontrolled study and in a five-hospital stepped evaluation, but unplanned intensive care admission did not change and death was too rare to compare. Simulation checklist scores predict real-call performance poorly, so real-call measures should carry the evaluation. Unannounced simulations can be stopped safely for real calls but cause anxiety among ward staff. Structured debriefing improves immediate learning, and simulations expose latent safety threats. Families describe confusion about the team's roles. Intracluster correlations from 22 hospitals give planning values for a stepped design with few hospitals.
gradeRationale: One multi-site stepped evaluation with imprecise estimates, uncontrolled single-site data and indirect evidence on debriefing and measurement; certainty that in-situ simulation shortens time to first critical intervention is low, and very low for patient outcomes.
summary: Eight retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims; certainty low.
